text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Conditional Probability and the Concept of Reduced Sample Space",
    "scope": "Introduces the formal definition of conditional probability when prior knowledge of an event occurring is given. Teaches how conditioning contracts the original sample space to a restricted subspace and modifies event probabilities accordingly. Works through two contrasting examples: a flight punctuality problem with joint empirical probabilities and a loaded die experiment illustrating probability re-weighting under a restricted space.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: $P(B|A) = \\frac{P(A \\cap B)}{P(A)}$, valid strictly when $P(A) > 0$",
      "Flight punctuality example: given $P(D)=0.83$, $P(A)=0.82$, and $P(D \\cap A)=0.78$, finding $P(A|D) = \\frac{0.78}{0.83} \\approx 0.94$ and $P(D|A) = \\frac{0.78}{0.82} \\approx 0.95$",
      "Loaded die sample space reduction: die where even outcomes have probability $2/9$ and odd outcomes $1/9$; original probability of a perfect square $P(B) = P(\\{1, 4\\}) = 1/3$",
      "Conditioning on $A = \\{4, 5, 6\\}$ (outcome > 3) contracts the sample space to $A$, yielding $B|A = \\{4\\}$ and $P(B|A) = \\frac{2/9}{5/9} = \\frac{2}{5} \\neq P(B)$, demonstrating dependency"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Independence of Two Events",
    "scope": "Defines independence between two events mathematically and intuitively as the condition where the occurrence of one does not alter the probability of the other. Distinguishes dependent events from independent events. Demonstrates with a fair die roll that events originating from the exact same physical trial can still be statistically independent.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of independence: events $A$ and $B$ are independent if and only if $P(B|A) = P(B)$ or equivalently $P(A|B) = P(A)$, provided conditional probabilities exist",
      "Definition of dependence: $A$ and $B$ are dependent whenever $P(B|A) \\neq P(B)$",
      "Fair die demonstration: $A = \\{2, 4, 6\\}$ (even, $P(A) = 1/2$), $B = \\{3, 6\\}$ (multiple of 3, $P(B) = 1/3$), intersection $A \\cap B = \\{6\\}$ ($P(A \\cap B) = 1/6$)",
      "Calculation: $P(A|B) = \\frac{1/6}{1/3} = \\frac{1}{2} = P(A)$, proving statistical independence between events on the identical sample space"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "The Multiplication Rule (Product Rule)",
    "scope": "Derives the general product rule for the intersection of two events from the definition of conditional probability. Demonstrates its symmetry and shows how it simplifies under independence to the direct product of marginal probabilities. Applies the rule to sampling without replacement and compound sequential experiments.",
    "key_points": [
      "General product rule: $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B)$ for any events with non-zero probabilities",
      "Special product rule for independent events: $A$ and $B$ are independent if and only if $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$",
      "Fuse box example (sampling without replacement): box with 20 fuses (5 defective), probability both of 2 randomly removed fuses are defective is $P(A \\cap B) = \\left(\\frac{5}{20}\\right)\\left(\\frac{4}{19}\\right) = \\frac{1}{19}$",
      "Two-bag transfer example: Bag 1 (4W, 3B), Bag 2 (3W, 5B); drawing black from Bag 2 after moving one ball is $P(B_1 \\cap B_2) + P(W_1 \\cap B_2) = \\left(\\frac{3}{7}\\right)\\left(\\frac{6}{9}\\right) + \\left(\\frac{4}{7}\\right)\\left(\\frac{5}{9}\\right) = \\frac{38}{63}$",
      "Independent emergency services example: fire engine availability $P(A)=0.98$, ambulance availability $P(B)=0.92$; joint availability is $P(A \\cap B) = (0.98)(0.92) = 0.9016$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "The Chain Rule and Mutual Independence for Multiple Events",
    "scope": "Extends the multiplication theorem to sequences of $k$ events using successive conditioning. Establishes the rigorous definition of mutual independence for collections of $n$ events, showing why pairwise or overall joint product conditions alone are insufficient. Solves a sequential card-drawing experiment using the extended chain rule.",
    "key_points": [
      "General chain rule: $P(A_1 \\cap A_2 \\cap \\dots \\cap A_k) = P(A_1)P(A_2|A_1)P(A_3|A_1 \\cap A_2) \\dots P(A_k|A_1 \\cap \\dots \\cap A_{k-1})$",
      "Successive card drawing example: drawing 3 cards without replacement where $A_1$ is a red ace ($2/52$), $A_2$ is a 10 or jack ($8/51$), $A_3$ is between 3 and 7 exclusive ($12/50$); $P(A_1 \\cap A_2 \\cap A_3) = \\left(\\frac{2}{52}\\right)\\left(\\frac{8}{51}\\right)\\left(\\frac{12}{50}\\right) = \\frac{8}{5525}$",
      "Insufficiency of product condition $P(A \\cap B \\cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C)$: counterexample where $A = B$ and $C = \\emptyset$ yields zero on both sides, yet $A$ and $B$ are dependent",
      "Definition of mutual independence: a collection $\\{A_1, \\dots, A_n\\}$ is mutually independent if for every subset $\\{A_{i_1}, \\dots, A_{i_k}\\}$ ($k \\le n$), $P(A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap A_{i_k}) = \\prod_{j=1}^k P(A_{i_j})$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "The Law of Total Probability",
    "scope": "Defines a partition of a sample space and formulates the Law of Total Probability. Provides the step-by-step formal mathematical proof based on decomposing an arbitrary event into disjoint intersections and applying finite additivity alongside the product rule. Establishes this theorem as the foundational denominator for Bayesian inversion.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of a partition: events $B_1, B_2, \\dots, B_k$ partition $S$ if they are pairwise mutually exclusive (disjoint) and their union equals $S$, with $P(B_i) > 0$",
      "Theorem statement: $P(A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i \\cap A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i)P(A|B_i)$ for any event $A \\subseteq S$",
      "Proof step 1: represent $A$ as the disjoint union $A = (B_1 \\cap A) \\cup (B_2 \\cap A) \\cup \\dots \\cup (B_k \\cap A)$",
      "Proof step 2: apply axiom of finite additivity for mutually exclusive events: $P(A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i \\cap A)$",
      "Proof step 3: substitute $P(B_i \\cap A) = P(B_i)P(A|B_i)$ via the product rule to complete the identity"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Bayes' Rule",
    "scope": "Introduces Bayes' Rule for updating prior probabilities into posterior probabilities given observed evidence. Formulates the theorem for a partition of hypotheses and supplies its complete formal derivation from the definition of conditional probability and the Law of Total Probability. Clarifies the role of priors, likelihoods, and normalizing constants.",
    "key_points": [
      "Theorem statement: for a partition $B_1, \\dots, B_k$ and evidence event $A$ with $P(A) > 0$, $P(B_r|A) = \\frac{P(B_r \\cap A)}{\\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i \\cap A)} = \\frac{P(B_r)P(A|B_r)}{\\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i)P(A|B_i)}$ for $r = 1, \\dots, k$",
      "Derivation: begins with definition $P(B_r|A) = \\frac{P(B_r \\cap A)}{P(A)}$, expresses numerator as $P(B_r)P(A|B_r)$, and expands denominator via the Law of Total Probability",
      "Structural components: prior probability $P(B_r)$, likelihood of evidence $P(A|B_r)$, total marginal probability of evidence $P(A)$, and posterior probability $P(B_r|A)$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Random Variables and Classification of Sample Spaces",
    "scope": "Establishes the formal definition of a random variable as a real-valued mapping from a sample space. Explains standard notation differentiating the random variable from its realized numerical values and shows how values define event subsets. Classifies sample spaces into discrete and continuous categories with concrete physical examples.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: a random variable $X$ is a function associating a real number with each outcome in sample space $S$, denoted $X: S \\to \\mathbb{R}$",
      "Notation convention: capital letter $X$ denotes the random variable; lowercase $x$ denotes a specific realized value",
      "Event correspondence: the event $X = x$ represents the subset $\\{\\omega \\in S : X(\\omega) = x\\}$; e.g., for testing 3 components ($S = \\{NNN, \\dots, DDD\\}$), $X=2$ corresponds to $\\{DDN, DND, NDD\\}$",
      "Examples: drawing 2 balls without replacement from urn with 4 red and 3 black balls yields $Y \\in \\{0, 1, 2\\}$; indicator random variable for component defectiveness with $X \\in \\{0, 1\\}$",
      "Discrete sample space: contains a finite number of elements or a countably infinite sequence with as many elements as whole numbers",
      "Continuous sample space: contains an uncountably infinite continuum of points, such as time until radioactive particle decay $S = [0, \\infty) \\subset \\mathbb{R}$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "Discrete Probability Distributions and Probability Mass Functions",
    "scope": "Defines the probability mass function (PMF) for discrete random variables and formalizes its mandatory mathematical properties. Illustrates distribution construction via a 3-coin toss experiment. Derives and computes the Hypergeometric PMF for sampling without replacement from a finite population.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: a function $f(x) = P(X = x)$ is a probability mass function (PMF) if $f(x) \\ge 0$ for all $x$, $\\sum_x f(x) = 1$, and $P(X = x) = f(x)$",
      "Coin toss model: tossing 3 fair coins yields 8 equally likely outcomes; number of heads $M$ has distribution $f(0)=1/8$, $f(1)=3/8$, $f(2)=3/8$, $f(3)=1/8$",
      "Combinatorial formula: number of combinations of $n$ distinct objects taken $r$ at a time is $\\binom{n}{r} = \\frac{n!}{r!(n - r)!}$",
      "Hypergeometric PMF: for population $N$ containing $K$ defectives and sample size $n$, $P(X = x) = \\frac{\\binom{K}{x}\\binom{N - K}{n - x}}{\\binom{N}{n}}$ for $x = 0, \\dots, \\min(K, n)$",
      "Laptop purchase calculation ($N=20, K=3, n=2$): $f(0) = \\frac{\\binom{3}{0}\\binom{17}{2}}{\\binom{20}{2}} = \\frac{68}{95} = \\frac{136}{190}$, $f(1) = \\frac{\\binom{3}{1}\\binom{17}{1}}{\\binom{20}{2}} = \\frac{51}{190}$, $f(2) = \\frac{\\binom{3}{2}\\binom{17}{0}}{\\binom{20}{2}} = \\frac{3}{190}$",
      "Verification: $\\sum_{x=0}^2 f(x) = \\frac{136 + 51 + 3}{190} = \\frac{190}{190} = 1$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "The Cumulative Distribution Function for Discrete Random Variables",
    "scope": "Defines the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for discrete random variables as the running accumulation of probabilities. Details its mathematical formulation as a piecewise step function defined over the entire real line. Constructs the explicit closed-form piecewise CDF for the laptop quality control distribution.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: $F(x) = P(X \\le x) = \\sum_{t \\le x} f(t)$ defined for all $-\\infty < x < \\infty$",
      "Step-function nature: constant between possible discrete values of $X$ with jump discontinuities equal to $f(x)$ at each supported point",
      "Piecewise evaluation for laptop purchase example: $F(x) = 0$ for $x < 0$; $F(x) = \\frac{136}{190}$ for $0 \\le x < 1$; $F(x) = \\frac{136+51}{190} = \\frac{187}{190}$ for $1 \\le x < 2$; $F(x) = \\frac{190}{190} = 1$ for $x \\ge 2$"
    ]
  }
]
